scope: Two additional living marine specimens for the species guide, optional identification practice and reef encounters. Newly paraphrased biology copy uses museum, aquarium, FAO and government research accounts. Observation prompts are instructions for studying the models, not claims that feeding, reproduction or scent responses are simulated.
iucnYearConvention: iucnYear records the assessment year. Banggai cardinalfish: EN, assessed 1 March 2007; the original assessment was amended in the 2025 Red List. The current IUCN DOI registration owned by IUCN and the current FishBase IUCN export corroborate the original date, but direct IUCN species-page access failed. Giant triton: no current global assessment located; SeaLifeBase’s current IUCN field reports Not Evaluated, so use NE and null year. An old 1983 IUCN Rare entry uses an obsolete category and must not be represented as a modern risk assessment.

specimens.name: Banggai cardinalfish
specimens.iucnCitation: Allen, G.R. & Donaldson, T.J. 2025. Pterapogon kauderni (amended version of 2007 assessment). The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species 2025: e.T63572A274966962.
marks: Silvery body crossed by three bold, black vertical bars
Small white spots decorate the body and most fins
Two separate dorsal fins: a tasseled front fin and a long, tapering second fin
A deeply forked tail and elongated lower anal fin create a pointed outline
specimens.role: Feeds on tiny crustaceans and other plankton around shallow reef and seagrass habitats.
specimens.fact: The father broods eggs and developing young in his mouth, then releases fully formed juveniles.
specimens.habitat: Calm, shallow reefs and seagrass beds native to Indonesia’s Banggai Archipelago; introduced populations also occur outside that natural range.
specimens.diet: Mainly copepods, with other small plankton and bottom-dwelling crustaceans also taken.
specimens.behavior: Often hovers in groups near shelter. Young fish can hide among long-spined sea urchins or anemone tentacles.
specimens.observe: Compare its three dark bars, white dots and long fin tips with the pajama cardinalfish’s single broad bar and spotted rear body.

claimSupport.iucnCategoryAndDate: dx-fishbase-banggai_cardinalfish IUCN 2025-2 export; dx-ga-banggai_cardinalfish corroborates EN

specimens.caution: The IUCN category is Endangered; NOAA’s separate U.S. Endangered Species Act category is Threatened. Do not confuse the two systems. This is not naturally widespread throughout the Indo-Pacific. White spot patterns vary between individuals. The model is not assigned a sex or brooding state, and group hovering is not a rigid synchronized school.

specimens.name: Giant triton (Triton’s trumpet)
marks: Large spiral shell with a tall, pointed spire and a swollen final whorl
Cream-coloured shell patterned with brown markings and spiral ridges
A broad, orange shell opening with a light-and-dark striped inner edge
The flared outer lip has small teeth along its inner edge
specimens.role: Predator of sea stars and other echinoderms. Its feeding alone is not enough to control crown-of-thorns outbreaks.
specimens.fact: Researchers have seen crown-of-thorns starfish move away from water carrying a triton snail’s scent.
specimens.habitat: Hard and sandy bottoms around coral reefs across the tropical Indo-Pacific.
specimens.diet: Sea stars, including crown-of-thorns, and other echinoderms such as sea cucumbers.
specimens.behavior: Uses scent to locate prey and hunts across the reef, often at night.
specimens.observe: Follow the spiral ridges toward the pointed tip, then turn the specimen to study the orange opening, striped edge and small lip teeth.

specimens.caution: NE means no current assessment is recorded here; it does not mean the species is secure. Do not translate an old Rare entry or national protection into a current IUCN threatened category. Shell colour, wear and surface encrusting life vary. Charonia variegata is a distinct Atlantic species; do not import its range or description. The canal at the front of the opening is short. Tritons eat crown-of-thorns, but AIMS explicitly cautions that predation alone cannot control outbreaks. Scent-based management remains research, not a demonstrated reef-wide solution.

banggai_cardinalfish.basis: An illustrative 7.5cm adult below the 8.6cm maximum. The full 0–16m metadata interval follows the FAO species account and current FishBase field guide; many native populations use much shallower water, often 0–5m. Neither interval is a hard physiological boundary.
banggai_cardinalfish.anatomy: Three black bars, variable white dot pattern, two separate dorsal fins, tasseled first dorsal, tapering second dorsal and anal fins, and deeply forked tail. No longnose or exaggerated snout. Enlarged mouth should not be used to assign a sex.
banggai_cardinalfish.motion: Gentle hovering near shelter and small local fin movements are illustrative. Existing animals must retain placement and seeds.

giant_triton.basis: A 30cm shell is consistent with living Australian Museum observations; Waikīkī Aquarium describes shells to50cm. The numeric interval uses SeaLifeBase as a clearly stated metadata source, corroborated for parts of that interval by aquarium and AIMS research records; it is not exhaustive.
giant_triton.anatomy: Tall pointed coiled spire, inflated final whorl, broad flat spiral sculpture, large orange aperture, thick flared lip with small inner teeth, and a short anterior siphonal canal. It should not resemble a queen conch with finger-like lip projections or a long-canal whelk.
giant_triton.motion: The foot stays grounded. Restrained tentacle/siphon movement is an illustrative current response; fast continuous shell spinning, free swimming and modeled prey consumption would be misleading.
